claims.text: The enhanced corrosion resistance of steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications is primarily governed by a dense Cr2O3-based passive film.
An optimized grain size or phase distribution promotes rapid chromium diffusion to damaged surface areas.
The passive film and optimized microstructure act synergistically to mitigate localized corrosion under combined high-temperature, corrosive, and irradiative conditions.
Steels employed in these applications typically have martensitic or austenitic microstructures.
These steels carry a naturally formed chromium-rich passive oxide film.
Heat treatment can alter grain size and phase distribution.
Temperatures of approximately 450–700 °C, corrosive salt environments, and controlled irradiation are representative of the targeted chemical-processing and nuclear-power operating environments.
Greater grain-boundary density and an appropriate phase distribution facilitate chromium diffusion to local damage sites.
A dense Cr2O3 surface layer inhibits further oxidation or corrosion.
The Cr2O3 layer forms rapidly under service conditions.
An optimized microstructure acts as a chromium reservoir that repairs or reinforces disrupted passive film.
Samples with intact passive films will have lower corrosion rates than samples with less protective oxide coverage.
An optimized microstructure will further reduce corrosion relative to a typically processed baseline microstructure.
Removing or disrupting the oxide film will accelerate corrosion even when the microstructure remains optimized.
The grain-size effect on corrosion can be nonmonotonic, with an intermediate grain size outperforming both fine- and coarse-grained material.
Long high-temperature exposures can produce phase instability and chromium-rich precipitation that may limit the proposed mechanism.
The interaction between irradiation damage and passive-film stability is not fully predictable under all service conditions.
